opus-5.5.text:
I think the appeal is actually very simple, and it's worth appreciating how powerful it was. Before pre-training scaling became the dominant paradigm, research was quite uncertain. You'd have an idea, you'd try it, maybe it works, maybe it doesn't, and it was hard to know how to allocate resources. Then something remarkable happened: people discovered a recipe. You take a large neural network, you take a lot of data, you take a lot of compute, and you get better results. And it's predictable. You can draw the curves.

That predictability is enormously appealing, especially to companies. If you're deciding how to invest a large amount of money, a low-risk way to turn resources into capability is incredibly attractive. Compare that to research, where you say, "We're going to give researchers money and hope they find something." Scaling says, "Put in more, get out more." So the word "scaling" itself became a kind of organizing principle. It told everyone what to do.

Another thing about pre-training specifically is that you don't have to think hard about what data to use. The answer is: all of it. Everything people have written, the whole projection of the world into text. You don't need to carefully design what the model learns from, which is very different from RL, where you have to choose environments and decide what you're training for.

But I think we're at a point where this is changing. Data is finite. At some point pre-training runs out of data, and then you have to ask what comes next. Some kind of souped-up pre-training, or RL, or something different. And compute is now so large that the question becomes whether another 100x of scale would transform everything, and I don't think that's obviously true anymore. So in a sense we're going back to an age of research, just with very big computers. The scaling era sucked the air out of the room. Everybody did the same thing. Now ideas matter again.

r001.rationale: It says “scaling” became an organizing principle that “told everyone what to do.”

r002.rationale: It describes the recipe of more network, data, and compute producing better results predictably, with visible scaling curves.

r003.rationale: It calls scaling a low-risk way for companies to invest because they can predict returns, contrasting this with funding research and hoping for a discovery.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the appeal of scaling pre-training is actually very simple, and that simplicity is a big part of it. Before scaling, machine learning research was this very open-ended activity where you had to come up with ideas, and most ideas didn't work, and it was unclear what to try next. Then scaling came along and said: here is a recipe. You take a big neural network, you take a lot of data, you take a lot of compute, you combine them, and you get something that is better than what you had before. And crucially, it kept working. You'd do it again with more compute and more data, and it would get better again.

That's extremely appealing from the point of view of directing work, because it tells you what to do. It converts a research problem into something closer to an engineering problem. It's a low-risk way of investing resources. If you're a company or a lab and you're trying to decide where to put your effort, having a recipe that reliably produces improvements is very attractive. You don't need to be lucky. You don't need a brilliant new idea every six months. You just need to execute.

There's also something deeper, which is that pre-training on human text puts a lot of structure about the world into the model. The data is produced by people, and people have knowledge, and the model absorbs a compressed version of that. So you're not just getting a bigger function approximator, you're getting something that knows things, and the more you scale, the more it knows and the more it can do. That felt, and still feels, like a very natural direction.

Now, the thing I'd add is that recipes like this have a lifespan. The pre-training recipe worked because there was a lot of data lying around and a lot of compute that could be applied to it. But data is finite. The internet is finite. So the question of what you do when the easy version of the recipe runs out, that becomes the interesting question. And I think we're now entering a period where scaling alone is not the whole story, and research matters again.

r001.rationale: The response says scaling supplied a recipe that “tells you what to do,” making it a clear direction for research.

r002.rationale: It describes the pre-training recipe as continuing to improve when more compute and data are applied.

r003.rationale: It calls scaling a “low-risk” investment with reliable improvements, contrasting it with open-ended research where most ideas failed.

astra-6.text:
I think the appeal is that it gives you a very clear recipe. You take a fairly simple objective—predict the next token—and you make the model bigger, give it more data, give it more compute, and it gets better. And it gets better at a surprisingly broad range of things, beyond what you might have expected from that objective.

That’s very attractive as a way to organize research. Normally, you have an idea, you try it, and maybe it works. With scaling, you have something much more predictable. You can make a credible argument that if you invest more resources, you’ll get a more capable system. You can organize a large engineering effort around that.

But there are two different questions: does this recipe work, and how far does it go? The fact that it has been remarkably successful doesn’t, by itself, settle the second question.

r001.rationale: It says scaling provides a “very clear recipe” and is an attractive way to organize research, giving a clear direction for what to pursue.

r002.rationale: It describes next-token prediction with more model size, data, and compute, and says the model gets better predictably.

r003.rationale: It says predictable scaling can support a large engineering effort and justify investing more resources, but it does not compare that investment’s risk to exploratory research or call it lower-risk.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the appeal is that it gives you a very simple recipe for making progress. You take a neural network, you train it on more data, you make it bigger, and you put more compute into the training. And, within a pretty broad range, it gets better.

That’s a remarkable thing to have in a research field. Normally, you have an idea, you try it, and maybe it works, maybe it doesn’t. With scaling, you can make a fairly substantial investment and have some confidence that you’ll get an improvement. So it becomes possible to organize a lot of engineering effort around it.

But the deeper appeal is that the task looks simple while the things you have to learn to do it well are not simple. You’re predicting the next word, but to predict it really well, you need to understand what produced the text. You need to learn something about the world. That creates the possibility that one training objective can produce a very wide range of capabilities.

r001.rationale: It describes scaling as a simple recipe for progress that makes it possible to organize substantial engineering effort around it.

r002.rationale: It says that using more data, a larger network, and more compute makes the model better within a broad range.

r003.rationale: It mentions confidence that investment will improve results, but does not identify companies or compare the investment risk with exploratory research.
